planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moderately fertile, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: Sesleria nitida forms a tight, evergreen tuft of narrow, shimmering gray-blue leaves with darker undersides, giving the whole clump a metallic sheen distinct from the greener Sesleria autumnalis. Slender flowering stems rise above the foliage in mid to late spring, carrying near-black spikelets that open into small white blooms before fading to tan seed heads. It thrives in lean, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil and tolerates both drought and heat once established, making it a durable edging or mass-planting grass for rock gardens and dry borders. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges to keep clumps looking tidy.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or divisions in spring after frost danger passes, in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun.

directions: Mesa Verde forms a fast-spreading, mat-like carpet of small jellybean-shaped, gray-green succulent leaves that develop burgundy overtones in cool fall weather. From late spring through summer it is smothered in coral-to-salmon, daisy-like flowers that open fully only in bright sun. Excellent winter drainage is the single most important factor for survival in colder zones, since wet soil during dormancy is far more damaging than cold air temperatures. Use it as a xeriscape groundcover, in rock gardens, or cascading over retaining walls where its rapid spread is an asset rather than a nuisance.
sources: Plant Select (Denver Botanic Gardens / Colorado State University)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in sharply drained, sandy or gritty soil in full sun; avoid heavy clay or winter-wet sites.

directions: Bred from Delosperma cooperi specifically to improve winter survival, Table Mountain forms a dense, low mat of fleshy foliage covered from early summer into fall with shimmering fuchsia-pink flowers that have pale white centers. It was one of the first hardy ice plants reliably rated to USDA zone 4-5 with adequate drainage, making it a benchmark introduction for cold-climate xeriscaping. Plant it on slopes, in raised beds, or gravel gardens where water drains away quickly, since standing winter moisture is the main cause of crown rot in this otherwise tough succulent. Deadheading is unnecessary, as spent blooms are quickly hidden by new flushes of flowers.
sources: Plant Select (Denver Botanic Gardens / Colorado State University)

planting.note: Set out plants or divisions in spring in well-drained, gritty soil in full sun to part shade.

directions: Mountain sandwort forms a dense, low evergreen cushion of small, glossy dark-green leaves that in late spring and early summer becomes almost entirely hidden beneath a flush of relatively large, pure white five-petaled flowers. Native to mountainous parts of Spain, Portugal, and France, it is at its best in gritty, well-drained soil and struggles in heavy clay or soggy winter conditions. Use it to soften the edges of paths and walls, tuck it into rock garden crevices, or let it spill over the tops of retaining walls; light shearing after flowering keeps the mat tight and can encourage a modest rebloom.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost or set out transplants around last frost date in average, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Zing Rose forms a dense, evergreen clump of dark green foliage that from late spring through summer is covered in deep rose-red, single blooms held just above the mat on short stems. Deadheading spent flowers encourages the heaviest early-summer flush to be followed by a second round of bloom in early fall. It thrives in average to lean, gritty, well-drained soil and resents wet winter conditions, making raised beds or slopes ideal sites. The nectar-rich flowers are a reliable draw for butterflies, and the tidy, low habit suits edging, rock gardens, and the front of a sunny perennial border.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: This vigorous, low-growing form of orange stonecrop emerges in spring with reddish-tinged new growth that matures to blue-green, scalloped foliage forming a dense, fast-spreading mat. Bright, starry yellow flowers cover the plant from early to midsummer and gradually take on pink and copper tones as they age, extending the display well past the main bloom period. It is exceptionally tolerant of heat, drought, and poor soil once established, and its dense habit makes it an effective, low-maintenance groundcover for slopes, edging, and green roofs. Shear back lightly after flowering if a tighter, more compact mat is desired.

planting.note: Set out container plants or divisions in late spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Smoke Signal is a strongly upright, columnar selection of the native prairie grass little bluestem, prized for its dramatic color progression through the season: foliage opens deep blue-green in spring, shifts to smoky purple by midsummer, and finishes in vivid red-orange fall color that persists into winter. Its narrow, non-flopping habit makes it more useful as a vertical accent or in tighter garden spaces than the straight species, which tends to splay open. It performs best in lean, well-drained soil and full sun, and like other little bluestem selections it is highly drought-tolerant once established and provides winter structure and seed for birds if left uncut until early spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in late spring once soil has warmed, in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Purple Tears arose as a chance seedling discovered by a noted Dutch garden designer, likely a natural cross involving 'Shenandoah', and shares that parent's tidy, upright clumping habit. Its lighter green foliage holds its color and texture later into the season than many switchgrass cultivars, and airy, gray-tipped flower panicles appear in late summer, maturing into showy purple-tinted seed heads that persist through fall. At roughly four feet tall, it is compact enough for smaller borders while still providing the see-through, movement-rich quality switchgrass is valued for. Leave the dried foliage and seed heads standing through winter for structure and songbird forage, then cut the clump back hard in early spring before new growth emerges.
